disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized by a persistent pattern of hyperactivity and impulsivity that interferes with functioning or development, with inattention symptoms often present but not predominant. Clinically, individuals may present with chronic restlessness, difficulty remaining seated or engaging in quiet activities, excessive talking, and impulsive actions that lead to social, academic, or occupational impairment. Symptoms usually begin in childhood, but in some people they are only recognized or become clinically significant later in life when environmental demands change or compensatory strategies fail. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, or personality disorders by its early onset, cross-situational persistence, and stable trait-like pattern of hyperactive/impulsive behavior rather than episodic or situationally bound disturbance.

narrative.stressor: Over the last couple of years, Norman’s primary care clinic began pushing more aggressive monitoring of his blood pressure and cholesterol, which meant a growing list of appointments, lab visits, and daily medication routines he was expected to follow. While he had always been a laid‑back, on‑the‑go sort of person, the increased medical demands after a mild cardiac scare about 14 months ago exposed how much he struggled to keep track of scheduled visits, instructions, and home monitoring, especially as he juggled organizing repair projects and game nights at the senior center. His cardiologist became frustrated when he repeatedly showed up late or not at all, and his nieces started expressing concern when he missed rides, double‑booked social events, and seemed unable to stick with the structured follow‑up plan despite understanding its importance. At a follow‑up visit where he joked that he “just can’t sit still long enough to deal with all this doctor stuff,” the cardiologist suggested a mental health evaluation, and Norman agreed after realizing his difficulty managing health routines was beginning to threaten both his independence and his ability to keep leading his community activities.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep forgetting my appointments and daily health stuff, even when I really try to stay on top of it.”

narrative.stressor: Marie had managed to get by in high school and early factory work by choosing hands‑on tasks and working alone, but about 14 months ago her plant upgraded to faster, more complex production lines and stricter safety protocols. As she moved into a technician role with hopes of promotion, she was expected to monitor multiple machines, respond to alarms, and sit through lengthy training sessions, all while maintaining flawless safety compliance and documentation. Her long‑standing tendency to act quickly and move from station to station became a liability: supervisors wrote her up for disrupting briefings, missing critical steps, and making impulsive adjustments that occasionally shut lines down, and she narrowly avoided a serious safety incident when she stepped into a restricted area without waiting for a lockout. After being put on a performance improvement plan and told that future certifications were at risk unless she could reliably stay focused and follow procedures, Marie sought psychiatric help at the urging of a union rep who wondered if there was an underlying attention disorder contributing to her escalating workplace problems.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to stay focused on what I’m doing at the machines long enough to do the job the way they need me to.”

narrative.stressor: Thomas was promoted from a largely analytical strategist role into a senior operations position about a year and a half ago, which dramatically changed his daily rhythm from quiet, self‑paced work to long leadership meetings, stakeholder calls, and constant decision‑making under time pressure. The new role required him to sit through hours of planning sessions, listen to detailed reports, and wait his turn in discussions, which clashed with his longstanding tendency to think and act quickly and to jump in as soon as ideas came to mind. Over the following year, colleagues began to comment that he cut people off in meetings, derailed agendas with side issues, and seemed unable to tolerate the slower pace of group processes, straining relationships with peers he otherwise cared about mentoring and supporting. When a trusted board member gently told him that his impatience and meeting behavior were starting to undermine his credibility despite strong performance metrics, Thomas sought a psychiatric consultation to understand why, despite meditation and self‑discipline, he felt so restless and unable to restrain himself in these structured settings.
narrative.chief_complaint: “In meetings I keep jumping in over people and cutting them off before I can stop myself.”
